blocks.text: The heat content or enthalpy H of a system combines two parts: that which is free to be converted to other forms of energy, the Gibbs free energy G, and that which is necessary to maintain the system at the specified temperature and is unavailable for conversion, T x S. So H = G + TS, and all of a system's enthalpy would be available only at zero kelvin. For two states, delta H = delta G + delta(TS); at constant temperature delta H = delta G + T delta S, or delta G = delta H - T delta S.
Spontaneity from the sign of delta G

items: Delta G negative (less than zero): the process may occur spontaneously.
Delta G positive (greater than zero): the process cannot occur spontaneously; its reverse may occur instead.
Delta G zero: neither the process nor its reverse occurs spontaneously; the system is at equilibrium.

blocks.caption: Sign of delta G = delta H - T delta S

blocks.prompt: A reaction has delta H greater than zero and delta S less than zero. Will it be spontaneous, and under what conditions of delta H and delta S is a reaction always spontaneous?
blocks.explanation: Never: both terms make delta G = delta H - T delta S positive at every temperature. A reaction is always spontaneous when delta H is negative and delta S is positive, because then delta G is negative whatever the temperature.

items: H = G + TS: G is the free part of the enthalpy, TS the part tied to temperature; delta G = delta H - T delta S at constant T.
Delta G negative: spontaneous; positive: not (the reverse may be); zero: equilibrium. Exothermic with rising entropy is always spontaneous; endothermic with falling entropy never.
